messages:
maria: Quick sync — we ran a pair of apples-to-apples load tests to compare streaming vs non-streaming with kernel selection and KV cache toggles. Wanted to share results and decide next experiment.:eyes:
kevin: nice, which harness did you use? replay or synthetic generator?
sasha: both. replay harness for real-client traffic shape, synthetic generator for controlled seq-len and token distro. kept same RNG seed for deterministic batching.
yun: can you paste the exact commands? want to reproduce locally.
sasha: sure — example command for the replay run:
```
./harness/replay \n  --model rwd-3b-q4 \n  --mode streaming \n  --concurrency 32 \n  --chunk-size 256 \n  --kv-cache enabled \n  --batch-window-ms 4 \n  --trace /tmp/run_trace.pb
```
sam: and non-streaming used the same but `--mode nonstream` and `--response-buffering enabled`, same concurrency.
perf-bot: run finished — metrics summary attached (p50/p95/p99 latency in ms, tokens/s): streaming(kv_on): 18/95/320, 12.1k tps; streaming(kv_off): 22/120/410, 9.7k tps; nonstream(kv_on): 26/110/380, 11.3k tps; nonstream(kv_off): 30/135/520, 10.2k tps.
jeff: interesting — KV cache improved tokens/s more for streaming. any kernel selection logs?
sasha: yes — runtime picked `kernels::fused_attn_short` for short-decoding paths when chunking is small; for non-streaming and long sequences it falls back to `kernels::matmul_multihead_v2`. The fused kernel had ~20% lower per-token latency when prefix hits were high.
maria: so kernel selection is sequence-length + KV-hit dependent. that explains streaming benefit: chunking keeps per-call seq small so runtime can prefer fused kernel.
kevin: what about batching heuristics? did you lock batch-window or let adaptive batching decide?
sasha: we tested three modes: fixed window 4ms, fixed window 12ms, and adaptive. Adaptive reduced p99 in high variance replay (few large requests) by avoiding huge batches that blow up tail latency. But it slightly reduced throughput (~3%).
yun: any backpressure from client read loops? we saw earlier that clients with busy event loops can starve the read and increase server-side inflight.
sasha: yep — we added a client-side delay model. When client read drain < 1ms it's fine. If client drains slowly (e.g., Node read loop blocked), streaming responses pile up and the server's streamer buffer hits the soft limit, causing backpressure and forced batching flushes -> higher tail latency.
sam: how did you simulate slow drains?
sasha: two modes: TCP-level pause (tc qdisc netem) and application-level sleep before read. both showed same pattern but app-level produced worse tails because it delayed acking more tokens.
perf-bot: flamegraph snippet (top stacks):
``
decode_step -> kv_lookup (20%) -> matmul (35%) -> residual_add (10%)
``
For fused kernel runs, `kv_lookup` drop to 12% and `fused_attn` dominates at 45%.
kevin: actionable takeaways?
maria: 1) For low-latency streaming, prefer small chunk sizes so runtime picks fused kernels when possible. 2) Keep KV cache primed for hot prefixes — big wins. 3) Adaptive batching with a max-window cap gives best p99 protection on varied workloads. 4) Document client read-loop best practices (drain quickly, avoid blocking ops).
jeff: add an experiment: force kernel selection overrides to validate perf delta end-to-end (A/B: force fused vs force matmul).
sasha: agreed — I'll schedule an A/B run and drop the results in the runbook: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/perf/replay-harness. Also will open a small PR to instrument streamer buffer watermarks in traces.
maria: thanks — and @kevin @yun please review the run config in the PR when it's up. :thumbsup:
kevin: will do.
